Sleep, food and comfort diary for families

A short diary can reveal questions worth discussing with a clinician. It cannot prove a food intolerance, biochemical subtype or cause of autism.

4 min read · Sources checked 26 October 2026 · Editorial information

Go to the worksheet

When sleep, eating and distress seem to change together, memory can blur the sequence. A brief diary helps a family describe what happened without having to decide in advance why it happened. It can be particularly useful when a child communicates discomfort through gestures, changes in activity or behaviour.

Use one printed sheet for a day and repeat for a few ordinary days if useful. This is not a food challenge, an elimination-diet protocol or a symptom score. Its purpose is to support a conversation with a clinician, dietitian or therapist.

What you will take away

  • Record ordinary routines, including days that go well.
  • Separate what you observed from what you think caused it.
  • Do not change medicines or restrict foods to test a theory through this diary.

In this guide

  1. What to record—and what to leave out
  2. A worked example of a neutral entry
  3. When recording should give way to seeking help
  4. Review the pattern with a clear question
  5. Printable worksheet
  6. Common questions

01

What to record—and what to leave out

Note bedtime and waking, meals and drinks accepted, bowel comfort, relevant medicines and changes in routine. Describe the child’s communication as accurately as possible: “pointed to stomach” is more useful than “gut inflammation”. A short note about the environment can matter as much as a food entry.

Avoid trying to count every movement, expression or mouthful. The diary should be sustainable and should not make the child feel watched throughout the day. If nothing unusual happened, record that too. A diary containing only difficult episodes can give an incomplete impression of the week.

02

A worked example of a neutral entry

Suppose a child becomes upset after lunch. The interpretation might be “dairy caused a meltdown”, but the observation could be: “Ate rice and curd at 1 pm. Fire alarm test at 1:20 pm. Cried and covered ears; settled in the quiet room after 15 minutes.” The second account preserves several possible explanations.

Another entry might say: “Woke three times overnight; hard stool in the morning; declined breakfast; said ‘tummy hurts’.” That gives the clinician a pattern to investigate without claiming that sleep, food or behaviour caused the others. Record a change recommended by a clinician along with its start date, but avoid making additional changes solely to create an experiment.

Bad dayNeeded a quiet break after assembly; joined art later

03

When recording should give way to seeking help

Do not delay care to obtain a complete week of notes. Persistent vomiting, blood in stool, dehydration, severe pain, concerning weight loss or a child who is markedly unwell needs medical advice. New neurological symptoms or loss of skills should be reported promptly.

Likewise, do not explain a new rash, pain or worsening function as beneficial detoxification. If a symptom appears after a treatment change, tell the prescriber or clinician what changed and when. The diary is supporting information, not permission to continue a concerning intervention.

04

Review the pattern with a clear question

At the end, choose the question the diary helps you ask. For example: “Could constipation be contributing to mealtime distress?” or “Does the sleep pattern need assessment?” Ask which findings need investigation and which everyday adjustments are reasonable.

Keep completed sheets private. Share only what is relevant with school or other professionals, and include the child in that decision where appropriate. Stop the diary when it has answered its purpose; long-term surveillance is not automatically more useful than a short, well-described period. The website does not collect your written entries.

  • Understand the difference between gut symptoms and diet claims

One day of observations

Print this page or save it as a PDF using your browser. Write on the printed copy. This page does not collect your answers.

Date and any change to the usual routine

Bedtime, waking time and overnight waking

Meals and drinks offered and accepted

Bowel movement and signs of pain or discomfort

Medicines or supplements taken as prescribed

Activity, noise, transitions and sensory demands

What the child said, showed or communicated

What helped comfort or participation

Questions for the next clinical conversation

Common questions

Does discomfort after a meal prove an intolerance?

No. Discuss a repeated pattern with a clinician rather than diagnosing from timing alone.
